title: That One breathed
hookLine: a still room and a baby breathing. Before day and night, the hymn says, That One breathed without wind: a seed of one reality, many names
carry: that one: one reality, before every name
tomorrow: dark hidden in dark. what made the first thing?

cards: A small room late at night. The window is shut. The fan is off.
Not a curtain moves. In a crib in the corner a baby is asleep, and the only motion in the room is the rise and fall of that tiny chest. No wind blows anywhere.
Nothing pushes that breath from outside. It comes from within, steady and quiet. A parent can stand there a long time, just listening.
The Nasadiya Sukta's second verse reaches for a stillness like that, before there was a night to sleep in, and finds a breath.

teach.b: The first verse cleared away being and non-being, air and sky. The second keeps clearing. In paraphrase: there was no death then, and no deathlessness.

teach.h: NO SIGN OF NIGHT OR DAY.
teach.b: No sign to tell night from day. Death and its opposite, the undying: gone. Night and day, the rhythm a life runs on: gone, or not yet.
And then, for the first time in the hymn, something is.
That One breathed, the verse says, without wind, by its own power. Apart from it, there was nothing else at all. Not a god with a name.
Not Agni, not Indra, not Varuna. Just That One, tad ekam. And not doing anything grand.
It breathes. Breath is life, but here there's no air, so the breath is windless, moved by nothing outside itself. Readers take That One in different ways.

Vedanta teachers in Shankara's line hear Brahman, prior to every name. Other Hindu readers hear the Lord before the work of creation. Some hear a poet pushing language as far as it goes and finding only a breath.
The verse doesn't decide for them. But here's what it plants.
A few days ago you met the verse that says what is one, the wise speak of in many ways.
This hymn reaches further back, before Agni, Indra or Varuna had names, to That One.
It's a seed of a teaching that runs all through Hinduism: many gods, many names, and one reality underneath, which the Upanishads will call Brahman.

how: Hindu teachers read the Nasadiya Sukta's 'That One' (tad ekam) in different ways: in Advaita Vedanta as Brahman beyond names, in devotional schools as the Lord before creation, and it is chanted as part of the Rig Veda's recited text.

games.q: you're the poet. there's no air, no sky, no night or day, no death. is anything there at all? what do you write?
o: That One breathed, without wind, by its own power.
games.why: the verse says That One breathed, windless, by its own power, and apart from it there was nothing else.

practice: Stop managing the breath: don't deepen it or slow it, just watch it go on its own, rising and falling with nothing outside pushing it, and rest in the stillness around it.
When the mind starts to explain the breath, let the explanation go and come back to the plain fact of it; if you pray, you can rest in that breath as a gift.

wordCard.voice: The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation, whose second verse says: no death, no deathlessness, no night or day, only That One, breathing without wind.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tad ekam, That One. What the Nasadiya Sukta's second verse says breathed, without wind.
